strengths: Introduces CRAFT, a real-time, real-world Chinese benchmark for knowledge editing in statistics and finance, with low exposure rates (Table 2) and an automatic update pipeline, addressing static/contaminated benchmarks.

Proposes new evaluation dimensions including composite reasoning portability over paired edits, alias portability, temporal locality, and common-sense locality, enabling more comprehensive assessment.
Provides extensive experiments comparing representative knowledge editing methods and reveals their limitations, plus ablation studies validating KEDAS components.
KEDAS integrates LoRA alignment, diverse edit augmentation, filter-based retrieval, and self-adaptive inference, achieving strong empirical gains on CRAFT and traditional benchmarks (Tables 5, 9).
Reproducibility is supported by public code/data, detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, computational budget, and deterministic generation.
weaknesses: Benchmark scope is narrow: Chinese language only and two domains (national statistics and finance), limiting broader relevance and cross-lingual/cross-domain conclusions.
The 'real-time' claim is somewhat overstated; updates are monthly/yearly snapshots rather than truly streaming, and the finance subset updates annually.

Key methodological details are missing or relegated to appendices: exposure-rate computation, exact composite reasoning metric, alias-list construction/validation, and filter training data generation are not fully specified in the main text.

Baseline comparisons may be insufficiently tuned (e.g., IKE only 8-shot, EREN default prompts) while KEDAS is trained and filtered on CRAFT's training set, so the reported gains may partly reflect benchmark-specific optimization.

Only one LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) is evaluated, limiting generalizability across model families and sizes; the method is also incremental over LTE and retrieval-based editing, with novelty largely in augmentation and filtering.

The paper lacks statistical significance tests and detailed error analysis; some results (e.g., KEDAS underperforming EREN on temporal locality for Finance) are only briefly explained without deeper investigation.
Potential temporal inconsistency in an appendix example (querying July 2025 outside the stated July 2024-June 2025 collection window) suggests minor data curation/verification issues.

strengths: Introduces CRAFT, a real-time, automatically updatable Chinese knowledge-editing benchmark sourced from official statistics/finance data, addressing the temporal staleness and contamination issues of static benchmarks.

Defines new evaluation dimensions (composite reasoning portability, alias portability, temporal locality, common-sense locality) that go beyond standard edit success/locality/portability and provide a more comprehensive assessment.

Proposes KEDAS, a well-motivated pipeline combining LoRA-based alignment, diverse edit augmentation, filter-based retrieval, and self-adaptive inference; the method achieves strong results on CRAFT and on traditional knowledge-editing benchmarks.
Ablation studies verify the contribution of each KEDAS component, and the appendix provides useful details: alignment data construction, prompts, hyperparameters, and dataset examples.
The paper is generally clear and reproducible: code/data/scripts are promised, deterministic evaluation is used, and limitations/ethical considerations are discussed.
weaknesses: The benchmark is limited to Chinese and two domains (national statistics and finance), with only 2-hop composite reasoning and annual finance updates; this narrow scope limits its broader adoption and generalizability to other languages/domains.

Experimental evaluation is restricted to a single LLM (Llama-3.1-8B) and a small test set (1,000 instances); no statistical significance tests or multiple model sizes are provided, so claims of significant superiority are not statistically supported.

The exposure-rate analysis in Table 2 is not fully described in the main text; low exposure for CRAFT may partly reflect domain difficulty rather than only data freshness, and the metric needs clearer validation.

The method is largely an integration of existing techniques (LoRA, retrieval, routing, data augmentation), with moderate novelty; there is no deeper analysis of why specific components interact as they do.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat constrained: several baselines are not designed for sequential real-time editing, hyperparameter tuning appears limited, and the same retrieval backbone as LTE is used for KEDAS, which may favor the proposed method.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code/data URL in the abstract (the link is not shown), and by reliance on external APIs and data sources (cn-stats, AKShare, GPT-4o-mini) that may change or become unavailable.

The common-sense locality evaluation draws on the C^3 dataset under a non-commercial license, and it is unclear how this subset can be redistributed within CRAFT; additionally, common-sense multiple-choice questions are only loosely related to knowledge editing.

strengths: Introduces CRAFT, a real-time, continually updatable knowledge-editing benchmark based on official Chinese statistics and financial data, addressing the staleness and contamination issues of static benchmarks such as ZsRE and MQuAKE.

Defines several useful evaluation dimensions beyond standard edit success, including composite reasoning portability, alias portability, temporal locality, and common-sense locality, with paired edits that make the benchmark more challenging than single-edit settings.
Provides low-exposure evidence across five LLMs (Table 2), supporting the claim that CRAFT is temporally fresh and less contaminated than existing benchmarks.

Proposes KEDAS, a practical combination of LoRA-based alignment, diverse edit augmentation, filter-based retrieval, and self-adaptive post-alignment inference, and reports consistent gains over representative baselines on CRAFT and traditional benchmarks (Tables 5 and 9).
Includes implementation details, prompt templates, and hyperparameters in the appendix, which are helpful for reproducibility if the promised code and data are released.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not adequately supported in the manuscript: the abstract says code and data are 'available at' but no actual URL, repository, or artifact link is provided. For a benchmark paper, this is a serious omission.

Evaluation is limited to a single LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). For a benchmark contribution, this is insufficient to claim that CRAFT is broadly challenging or that existing methods have inherent limitations; results may not generalize to other open or closed models.

The conceptual framing is questionable: because CRAFT facts are mostly post-training numeric statistics and financial values with near-zero exposure, the task may be closer to knowledge injection/retrieval-augmented QA than editing outdated internal knowledge. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish these settings.

Composite reasoning portability conflates knowledge editing with arithmetic and multi-hop reasoning. For example, the debt-ratio query requires combining two edits and performing division, so failures may reflect math or reasoning errors rather than knowledge-editing failures.

Method novelty is incremental: KEDAS largely combines existing components (LoRA alignment from LTE, retrieval, a relevance filter, and LLM-based edit augmentation). The largest gains appear to come from routing irrelevant queries to the frozen base model, which can make locality near-perfect by construction.

The ablation study raises concerns about what the locality metric actually measures: removing self-adaptive post-alignment inference drops temporal/common-sense locality from 100% to roughly 5–11%, while edit success and portability remain almost unchanged. This suggests the locality advantage is mainly a routing artifact.

Experimental rigor is limited: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported, and baseline tuning appears uneven (e.g., IKE is evaluated in 8-shot mode and EREN uses its default prompt).

Dataset construction details are underspecified: the main paper does not clearly describe train/test splits, temporal leakage controls, how exposure rates are computed, or whether test facts are disjoint from training edits.

Several claims are overstated: KEDAS does not achieve 'outstanding performance in all metrics' (e.g., IKE has higher edit success on both CRAFT subsets), and the reported composite-reasoning gains are moderate rather than decisive.
The benchmark is limited to Chinese statistics and finance, and the paper does not demonstrate cross-lingual or cross-domain generality, which limits its broader relevance to the NLP community.

strengths: Introduces CRAFT, a real-time, contamination-free Chinese knowledge editing dataset built from continuously updated official statistics and finance sources; exposure analysis shows near-zero leakage across multiple LLMs, directly addressing a key weakness of static benchmarks.

Proposes KEDAS, a well-motivated pipeline combining LoRA-based alignment, diverse edit augmentation, filter-based smart retrieval, and self-adaptive post-alignment inference, with an explicit aim to balance edit success, locality, and portability.

Provides extensive experiments on both CRAFT and KnowEdit across multiple open-source LLMs, including ablations that isolate the contribution of diverse edit augmentation, the filter, and self-adaptive inference.

Offers new evaluation dimensions tailored to real-time editing, including composite reasoning portability, alias portability, temporal locality, and common-sense locality, which go beyond standard edit-success/locality/portability metrics.
Reproducibility is generally strong: public code and data, detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, implementation details, artifact licenses, and a limitations section.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a useful comparison of existing datasets and a clear statement of the intended real-time knowledge editing setting.
Empirical results on CRAFT and KnowEdit show KEDAS achieving strong and balanced performance relative to representative baselines such as IKE, EREN, WISE, LTE, ROME, and LoRA.
weaknesses: The CRAFT dataset is restricted to Chinese national statistics and finance; the paper does not empirically demonstrate that its real-time or contamination-free properties generalize to other languages, domains, or knowledge types.

The main sequential-editing experiments omit several strong or contemporary knowledge editing baselines (e.g., MEMIT, AlphaEdit, MEND, SERAC, RECIPE) because of compatibility/cost issues; these are only partially evaluated under single editing in the appendix, weakening the comparative claim that existing methods exhibit inherent limitations.

The 'real-time' dataset is still a snapshot at publication; although update scripts are provided, the official data update cadence (monthly/annual) may not fully represent continuously evolving knowledge, and the current evaluation is on a fixed version.

No statistical significance tests, variance estimates, or repeated runs are reported; given the strong headline results for KEDAS, single-run evaluations and sensitivity to retriever/filter/prompt choices are not fully addressed.

KEDAS depends on GPT-4o-mini for diverse edit augmentation and a trained BERT-based filter; this introduces reliance on proprietary API access, possible non-determinism, and a filter bottleneck, with limited analysis of failure modes when the filter or augmentation is unavailable or noisy.

Some evaluation metrics are brittle or under-specified: exact match for numerical answers may be overly strict, alias portability relies on a manually curated alias list, and composite reasoning portability is limited to two-hop reasoning.

The paper's central claim that KEDAS is an 'ideal paradigm' is supported mainly by benchmark scores; there is limited qualitative analysis of when and why the filter/retriever and self-adaptive inference succeed or fail in realistic streaming edit scenarios.

Certain methodological details needed to assess sequential editing are deferred to the appendix or remain unclear in the main text, such as the exact order/number of edits applied during evaluation, how train/test splits interact with memory construction, and whether any test-set edits are used for retrieval training.

strengths: Introduces CRAFT, a real-time, contamination-free Chinese knowledge editing dataset built from continuously updated official statistics and financial data, with low exposure rates and comprehensive evaluation dimensions including composite reasoning portability, alias portability, and temporal/common-sense locality.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation of representative knowledge editing methods on both CRAFT and traditional KnowEdit datasets, revealing limitations and tradeoffs among edit success, locality, and portability.

Proposes KEDAS, a well-motivated framework combining LoRA-based alignment, diverse edit augmentation, filter-based smart retrieval, and self-adaptive post-alignment inference, achieving strong and balanced performance across metrics with ablation support for each component.

Reproducibility is generally strong: code and data are stated to be publicly available, hyperparameters and prompt templates are provided, artifact licenses are listed, and computational budget is described.
Clear presentation, useful dataset comparison (Table 1), and thorough appendix with implementation details, prompts, and additional results.
weaknesses: The dataset and evaluation are restricted to Chinese national statistics and finance; the claim that the methodology is universal is not empirically validated across other languages or domains, limiting broader impact.

The filter-based retriever setup is unclear or inconsistent for the English KnowEdit experiments: a Chinese BERT filter trained on CRAFT is specified, but how it applies to English datasets is not explained, raising reproducibility and validity concerns for cross-dataset results.
The proposed method relies on GPT-4o-mini for edit augmentation and manually curated alias lists; robustness to API changes, prompt variation, and different domains is not established.
Automatic exact-match metrics for numerical/financial QA may not fully capture semantic correctness; no human evaluation or detailed error analysis is provided.
The 'real-time' property is tied to a specific data collection window (July 2024–June 2025); while update scripts are provided, the dataset's freshness at publication time may be limited.
Composite reasoning portability is only 2-hop, as acknowledged, which limits assessment of deeper multi-hop reasoning.
Some recent baselines (e.g., MEMIT, AlphaEdit, SERAC, MEND) are omitted from the main tables due to compatibility/cost, so the main comparison is not exhaustive.

strengths: Introduces CRAFT, a Chinese real-time knowledge-editing dataset built from continuously updated official sources (National Bureau of Statistics, AKShare), with an API-driven pipeline that makes it extensible and genuinely distinct from static Wikipedia-based benchmarks.

Provides a useful exposure analysis (Table 2) showing that existing benchmarks are heavily contaminated (22-76% for MQuAKE-T, ZsRE, etc.) while CRAFT is near-zero exposure, which is good evidence for the 'real-time/contamination-free' claim.

Systematic evaluation of representative KE methods (LoRA, ROME, IKE, EREN, WISE, LTE) across edit success, locality, portability and the newly proposed composite/alias/temporal/common-sense metrics, clearly exposing trade-offs between edit success and locality.
Reproducibility is comparatively good: public code/data, explicit hyperparameters (Table 9), prompt templates (Figures 2-3), ablation study (Table 7) and per-subset statistics (Table 3).
KEDAS is simple and reproducible, and the results are consistent across CRAFT and KnowEdit as well as across several LMs (Tables 5, 6, 11, 12).
weaknesses: The edit-success (ES) metric on CRAFT is largely a numeric-copying task. For retrieval-based methods (IKE, KEDAS) the edit is placed in the prompt, so the ~99-100% ES is trivially achieved and uninformative; the benchmark's real discriminative power collapses onto locality, which is produced by a separate relevance classifier rather than by the editing mechanism.

KEDAS is an incremental combination of existing ideas (LoRA alignment from LTE, retrieval from IKE/EREN, a relevance filter and prompt-based edit augmentation), with limited technical novelty. 'Self-adaptive post-alignment inference' is essentially relevance/OOD-based routing, not a new editing paradigm.

The near-perfect locality (100% L_common) is an artifact of the BERT-based filter that distinguishes in-scope from out-of-scope (e.g., C^3) queries; the ablation (Table 7) shows that removing the filter drops locality to ~5-11%, indicating the classifier, not the editing, is responsible for locality. This makes the locality claims much weaker than presented.
The dataset is small (4,468 + 7,800 instances; only 1,000 test items) and restricted to two narrow Chinese domains; this limits generality and statistical power.

There is an inherent tension between the 'real-time, auto-updating' property and benchmark stability/reproducibility: results collected at different times are not comparable, and the paper does not discuss how this is handled.

Composite-reasoning portability on CRAFT-Finance reduces to arithmetic (e.g., computing a debt-to-asset ratio from two edits), conflating numerical reasoning with knowledge editing, and is only 2-hop.

Evaluation on CRAFT uses only two small models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-3B), and several relevant baselines (MEMIT, AlphaEdit, MEND, SERAC, RECIPE) are excluded for resource/compatibility reasons, weakening the comparative claims.

The exposure analysis may overstate the novelty of CRAFT's knowledge: the targets are arbitrary monthly/periodic numbers that no model would memorize regardless of whether the underlying concepts are known, so near-zero exposure does not by itself establish that the evaluated knowledge is 'new'.

The framing of 'real-time knowledge editing' conflates retrieval-based in-context use with parametric editing; for the best-performing methods nothing is actually edited in the model, so the paper's central framing is somewhat oversold.
